case.case_title: Chandra Kalyanie Perera and Another v. Captain Siriwardena and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 27/90, decided on 30 and 31 January 1991

clause.text: No person shall be arrested except according to law and must be informed of the reason.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the arrest of the 1st petitioner was lawful under Article 13(1) of the Constitution, specifically if it was according to law and if she was informed of the reason for arrest.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The 1st petitioner claimed illegal arrest and detention, alleging she was not informed of the reason for arrest and was subjected to ill-treatment.
case_context.respondent_argument: The State argued the arrest was lawful under Regulation 18(1) of the Emergency Regulations based on reasonable suspicion of involvement in offences under Emergency Regulations, and that the petitioner was informed of the reason upon arrival at the army camp.
key_facts: The 1st petitioner was arrested on 29.01.90 by the army under Regulation 18(1) of the Emergency Regulations.
She was suspected of instigating the murder of her driver and assisting subversive activities.
The arresting officers informed her of the reason for arrest immediately upon arrival at the army camp.
There was credible material (statements and investigations) justifying a reasonable suspicion for arrest.
The 2nd petitioner was arrested with her but released the next day.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: Article 13(1) requires that any arrest be according to procedure established by law and that the person arrested be informed of the reason. The Court held that the test for lawful arrest is whether there was material for a reasonable officer to cause the arrest, not proof of commission of an offence. A reasonable suspicion based on credible material suffices. The Court recognized a wider discretion during emergency periods.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the 1st petitioner’s arrest was based on credible material including statements linking her to the murder and subversive activities. Although the army may have failed to inform her at the moment of arrest, they informed her immediately upon arrival at the camp. Therefore, the arrest was lawful and not violative of Article 13(1).
principles_established: Lawful arrest requires reasonable suspicion based on credible material, not proof of offence.
During emergencies, police and army have wider discretion in arrests.
Informing the arrested person of the reason is essential, but can be immediate upon arrival at detention.

outcome.holding: The Court held that the arrest of the 1st petitioner was lawful and not in violation of Article 13(1) of the Constitution.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(1) directly governs the legality of arrests and the requirement to inform the arrested person of the reason, which was central to the Court's determination of the lawfulness of the 1st petitioner's arrest.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court found credible material for reasonable suspicion and noted the petitioner was informed of the reason for arrest immediately upon arrival at the army camp.
